subject: Communication
title: Status and Power: Who Gets Listened To?
description: A short lesson to help you apply Status and Power: Who Gets Listened To?.

hook.text: In meetings, the highest-paid person's opinion often wins — regardless of quality.

buildup.text: We listen more attentively to people with higher status, authority, or perceived expertise — even when they're wrong.

discovery.text: Conversely, we dismiss ideas from lower-status speakers. Nurses who noticed medical errors were often ignored by doctors.

twist.text: Power also corrupts the powerful listener. High-power individuals interrupt more, listen less, and are more likely to dismiss.

climax.text: Organizations that flatten listening hierarchies — where anyone can be heard — make fewer errors and innovate faster.

punchline.text: The best ideas don't always come from the top.

quiz.question: How does power affect listening behavior?
options: High-power individuals interrupt more and listen less
Power has no effect on listening

details.summary: Social status profoundly influences who gets heard. Higher-status individuals receive more listening attention, more follow-up questions, and more charitable interpretation. Lower-status speakers are interrupted more, their ideas attributed to others, and their expertise doubted.
details.whyItMatters: Listening inequity perpetuates power imbalances in organizations and society. Awareness of status bias is the first step toward equitable communication.
takeaways: Higher-status speakers receive more attentive listening
Lower-status speakers get interrupted and overlooked more often
Conscious effort is needed to listen equitably across status

faq.question: How does gender affect who gets listened to?
faq.answer: Research consistently shows women are interrupted more, their ideas claimed by others more often, and their expertise questioned more frequently. In mixed groups, men's contributions receive more attention. These patterns persist even when women hold leadership positions.

faq.question: How can leaders ensure everyone gets heard?
faq.answer: Explicitly invite quieter voices to speak. Credit ideas to their original source. Notice and interrupt interruption patterns. Use structured turn-taking in meetings. Evaluate your own bias by noting whom you give sustained attention to versus whom you tune out.
